# Directory models

These are the directory models, in reading form. Each heading is
one TypeSpec model. [Abstract data model](data-model.md) is the
picture. [LDAP schema](ldap-schema.md) explains the names. The
directory still enforces nothing.

A value is **one**, **several**, or **not stated** when the model
does not say. A name's origin is **RFC**, **other standard**,
**this service**, **derived**, or **not stated**. **Secret** marks
a value the model withholds.

An OID that begins `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473` is a placeholder. That is the
number RFC 5612 reserves for documentation, and this service's own
names use it until its Private Enterprise Number is assigned.

This page is rewritten whenever that TypeSpec model is written.
Do not edit it by hand.

| `appFederationAutoRedirect` | one | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.21` | TRUE if a person signing in to this application should be sent STRAIGHT to the partner named above, without the sign-in screen in between. This is home realm discovery done by configuration instead of by asking, which is what a deployment with one federated identity provider actually does.  It is TRUE BY DEFAULT once a relationship is named, because naming one and then having to click a button is the state nobody wants; set it FALSE to keep the screen, where the partners are then the only buttons offered. An absent value therefore means "yes" here and not "unknown", which is the opposite of what RFC 7591 section 2 makes an omitted boolean mean — said out loud because the two rules meet on one entry.  WITH SEVERAL RELATIONSHIPS NAMED IT MEANS EXACTLY WHAT IT ALWAYS MEANT — "without the sign-in screen" — and what changes is what that leaves. With one it is a redirect straight to the partner. With several it is the chooser at /authn/select-idp: one button per partner and no password field, which is the sign-in screen's job done without the sign-in screen. What it never means is "pick one for them"; there is no value of a boolean that can say which identity provider somebody's employer is.  FALSE with several named is therefore the SCREEN, with one button per partner under the password box — the same thing FALSE has always done, with the partners plural.  With no relationship named it does nothing at all, rather than being an error: the two are edited separately and a value left behind by a relationship that was cleared should not refuse the next write. From the console, the management API, or by hand. |

| `appFederationRelationship` | several | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.24` | THE FEDERATION RELATIONSHIPS THIS APPLICATION'S USERS ARE AUTHENTICATED THROUGH — each value the `fedId` of an entry under ou=federations, in THIS trust realm, whose `fedRole` is service-provider. Both halves of that are checked when it is read rather than when it is written: an identity-provider-side relationship goes the other way (this service asserts to that partner, so there is nothing to sign in to), and the register is per realm, so an id that names a relationship in another realm names nothing here.  IT HOLDS A LIST, and that is what makes an application able to offer more than one identity provider. ONE usable value with the auto-redirect on is the case this attribute was added for and it is unchanged: the browser goes straight to that partner. SEVERAL usable values draw /authn/select-idp, where the person chooses which one — home realm discovery narrowed to this application's partners rather than performed against every relationship this service has. They need not share a protocol: a SAML 2.0 partner and an OpenID Connect one are two values here and two buttons there, because what the list names is where a person can be authenticated and not how.  A value that names a relationship this service cannot use is REPORTED on the screen rather than dropped, one line per value: a list of three whose middle entry is disabled must not look like a list of two.  It is WRITTEN BY NOBODY. No protocol presents it and no sighting derives it — an application's home identity provider is an arrangement somebody made, not something this service can observe — so it is editable and it starts empty. From the console, the management API, or by hand. |

| `oauthAllowedScope` | several | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.212` | THE SCOPES THIS CLIENT MAY BE ISSUED — RFC 7591 section 2's `scope`, "the list that the client can use when requesting access tokens". | `oauthPermission` | several | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.276` | ONE PERMISSION THIS APPLICATION EXPOSES, one value each. The value is the permission's NAME — `read`, `write`, `Widgets.ReadWrite.All` — optionally followed by `\|` and a description: `write\|Change widgets on somebody's behalf`. The FIRST `\|` is the delimiter and every later one belongs to the description, so a description may contain the character and a name may not.  The name must be a legal OAuth scope token (RFC 6749 section 3.3 — no space, no double quote, no backslash), because that is what a client will put in a `scope` parameter and what comes back on the token's `scope` claim. A name or a description containing an operator error code is refused too: both are returned on every page that lists the permission, and a code is recorded rather than sent. Nothing enforces either rule when an `ldapmodify` writes the value; this module and both consoles do.  A PERMISSION MUST EXIST BEFORE ANYTHING CAN BE GRANTED IT, which is the one ordering rule this feature has and is checked in updateApplication() so that the console form and the management API cannot disagree about it. It is checked on the GRANT and not here: this attribute is the definition, and a definition nobody has used yet is the ordinary first step rather than a mistake. From the console, the management API, or by hand. |
| `oauthPermissionBaseUri` | one | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.277` | THE BASE URI EVERY PERMISSION THIS APPLICATION DEFINES HANGS OFF, and the thing that makes a permission name globally unique here. Entra ID calls it the Application ID URI and spells it `api://<guid>`; the shape is the same and nothing here requires that scheme.  IT IS NORMALISED TO END IN A SEPARATOR when it is written through this module — a trailing `/` is added where there is no `/`, `#` or `:` at the end — because base + name is a plain concatenation and `https://example.com` + `write` would otherwise produce `https://example.comwrite`. An `ldapmodify` reaches this attribute like every other and is not normalised, so a base written by hand means exactly what it says.  SINGLE-VALUED, and it is the one attribute in this group that could not be widened without deciding something: two bases would mean every permission on the entry had two identifiers, and the lookup that turns a scope into an audience would have to pick one to put in `aud`. From the console, the management API, or by hand. |

| `samlSpMetadata` | one | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.378` | THE SERVICE PROVIDER'S METADATA DOCUMENT, cached verbatim. It is what the refresh action stores, and what uploading one on the SAML 2.0 page (or POST /admin-api/saml2/upload-metadata) stores for a service provider whose metadata this service cannot reach. CONSUMING it (2026-09-17) writes its AssertionConsumerService and SingleLogoutService endpoints as REGISTERED return addresses (samlAssertionConsumerService, samlAcsEndpoint, samlSingleLogoutService, samlSloEndpoint), its signing certificates (samlSigningCertificate), its encryption certificate (samlEncryptionCertificate), its NameIDFormats, AuthnRequestsSigned and WantAssertionsSigned, and its validUntil and cacheDuration. Setting this attribute by hand stores the document and consumes NOTHING — use the upload.  IT IS KEPT AS WELL AS THE EXTRACT so that a reader can see what was actually consumed. A certificate with no document behind it is a value nobody can check. From a metadata fetch, or by hand. |
| `samlSpMetadataCacheDuration` | one | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.379` | The EFFECTIVE cacheDuration of the consumed document (the shortest in its chain), as the xs:duration it carried. Once it has elapsed since the document was consumed, the document is STALE: the background refresher fetches it again where it can (saml2.spMetadataRefresh), and it keeps working until its validUntil. From consumed metadata. |
| `samlSpMetadataConsumedAt` | one | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.380` | When the document was last consumed, and how: `<ISO instant> <refresh\|upload\|mdq>` — `mdq` for one fetched from the Metadata Query responder, which the background refresher can fetch again. From consumed metadata. |
| `samlSpMetadataSignature` | one | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.381` | What checking the consumed document's own signature found: `verified`, `unsigned`, or `signed-not-verified` (signed, and no samlSpMetadataSigningCertificate to check it against). From consumed metadata. |
| `samlSpMetadataSigningCertificate` | one | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.382` | THE CERTIFICATE THIS SERVICE PROVIDER'S METADATA MUST BE SIGNED WITH, base64 DER. With it set, a document that is unsigned, or whose signature does not verify against it, is REFUSED and nothing on the entry changes. Without it a signed document is consumed and recorded as signed-not-verified: the trust act is then the operator's choice of URL (or document), which is what an explicit refresh or upload is. From by hand. |
| `samlSpMetadataUrl` | one | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.383` | WHERE THIS SERVICE PROVIDER'S METADATA IS PUBLISHED. It is fetched by the "refresh metadata" action on the application page and by POST /admin-api/applications/refresh-metadata, and NEVER while a flow is running — an assertion that had to wait on somebody else's web server to be issued would make every sign-in as reliable as that server. What the fetch writes is everything consuming the document writes — see samlSpMetadata below.  This is the SECOND outbound-request surface in this service; federation was the first and is the only other. It follows the same refusals — the URL must be one this entry carries, the scheme must be http or https, and the request times out. From by hand. |
| `samlSpMetadataValidUntil` | one | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.384` | The EFFECTIVE validUntil of the consumed document — the earliest on any enclosing EntitiesDescriptor, the EntityDescriptor and its SPSSODescriptor. A document already expired is refused when consumed; once this passes, every request from the service provider is REFUSED (STS-SAML-0074) until a newer document is consumed. From consumed metadata. |
| `samlSpNameIdFormat` | several | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.385` | The <md:NameIDFormat> values the service provider's metadata declares. Unlike samlNameIdFormat (what it has ASKED for), these RESTRICT: a NameIDPolicy naming another format is answered InvalidNameIDPolicy (saml-core-2.0-os section 3.4.1.1), and the default format is chosen from them. From consumed metadata. |
| `samlSpWantAssertionsEncrypted` | one | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.386` | TRUE when the consumed metadata publishes a KeyDescriptor marked use="encryption" — the service provider saying it has a key for encrypted assertions, which SAML 2.0 metadata has no attribute of its own for (the interoperability profiles read the key as the request). The assertion is then ENCRYPTED to that key in every mode, whatever saml2.encryptAssertion says. From consumed metadata. |
| `samlSpWantAssertionsSigned` | one | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.387` | TRUE when the metadata says WantAssertionsSigned="true": the assertion is signed even where saml2.signAssertion (or saml2SignAssertion) is off — in product mode; development honours the setting, which is a test case, and logs that the service provider asked otherwise. From consumed metadata. |
| `scepAllowedProfiles` | several | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.388` | THE SCEP PROFILES THIS APPLICATION MAY BE ISSUED. Where it lists something it OVERRIDES scep.allowedProfiles for this application, wider or narrower; empty leaves the realm's list. The five CA, OCSP and KDC profiles are never issued. From the console, or by hand. |
| `scepCertificateLifetimeDays` | one | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.389` | How long a certificate this application is issued over SCEP is valid, in days, overriding scep.certificateLifetimeDays (longer or shorter). No certificate outlives its Issuing CA. From by hand. |
| `scepDefaultProfile` | one | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.390` | THE PROFILE THIS APPLICATION IS ISSUED OVER SCEP WHEN A REQUEST NAMES NONE, overriding scep.defaultProfile. Used only while the list in force for it allows it. From the console, or by hand. |
| `scimClientAuthMethod` | one | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.391` | Families: scim-client. HOW A REQUEST IS AUTHENTICATED (RFC 7644 section 2): basic (HTTP Basic with scimClientUsername and scimClientPassword), oauth2 (a client_credentials token from scimClientTokenEndpoint, sent as a Bearer token), or none (only the TLS client certificate, when one is configured). From Protocols → SCIM → Clients, or by hand. |
| `scimClientBaseUrl` | one | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.392` | Families: scim-client. | `scimClientCaCertificates` | one | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.393` | Families: scim-client. | `scimClientDeprovision` | one | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.395` | Families: scim-client. | `scimClientGroupMode` | one | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.397` | Families: scim-client. | `scimClientId` | several | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.399` | WHAT A PROVISIONING CLIENT AT /scim/v2 IS CALLED — the OAuth client_id it presents a token from, or the username it sends in Basic. From the console, or by hand. |
| `scimClientJurisdiction` | one | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.400` | Families: scim-client. WHERE THE SERVICE PROVIDER IS, as a jurisdiction code of the cell map (us, eu, ca, …). Empty is an unknown jurisdiction, which the strict default never releases to. Ignored when the service is one cell. From Protocols → SCIM → Clients, or by hand. |
| `scimClientMaxRequestsPerSecond` | one | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.401` | Families: scim-client. HOW MANY REQUESTS A SECOND the service provider is sent, at most: every delivery, lookup, discovery read and reconciliation page waits for its turn rather than failing. | `ssfAllowedEvents` | several | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.463` | Families: ssf. WHICH SHARED SIGNALS EVENT TYPES A STREAM OWNED BY THIS APPLICATION MAY BE SENT. One value per line, each either a whole profile — `caep` (the eight session events) or `risc` (the fourteen account events) — or one event type URI, such as https://schemas.openid.net/secevent/caep/event-type/session-revoked. EMPTY MEANS UNRESTRICTED. SSF's own verification and stream-updated events are always allowed. It is ENFORCED twice: a stream this application creates or updates is agreed only the types allowed here (anything else it asked for is absent from `events_delivered`, and the stream's log says why), and every delivery checks it again, so removing a value stops existing streams receiving that type. The owner is whoever authenticated to /ssf/stream, matched against this entry's identifier or its ssfReceiverId values. From the console, the management API, or by hand. |

| `ssfReceiverId` | several | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.479` | WHAT A SHARED SIGNALS RECEIVER IS CALLED — whatever it authenticated as when it created a stream at /ssf/stream, which is also the `aud` of every Security Event Token that stream carries. It is separate from saml11AssertionLifetimeMin: one application may speak both, and a WS-Federation session and a Browser/POST assertion are not consumed the same way. From by hand. |

It was written into samlAssertionConsumerService until 2026-08-25, which put a wreply in the attribute the SAML pages read for an assertion consumer service and for the Single Logout fallback — one attribute holding two protocols' return addresses, so a WS-Federation application appeared to have a SAML ACS it had never named. Two facts, two attributes. Like the SAML one beside it this is CHECKED IN PRODUCT MODE ONLY: development refuses no wreply, because a service that refused would remove a test case rather than add one; product posts only to an address on this list and a sighting never adds one. A wreply development recorded is marked on appReturnAddressObserved and product refuses it until it is confirmed; values recorded before that mark existed carry none and still need reviewing before a realm is switched to product. From WS-Federation, the console, or by hand. |
| `wsfedSignOutUri` | several | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.703` | WHERE A wsignoutcleanup1.0 PING IS SENT for this application — WS-Federation's logout URI, and the one this table did not have until 2026-08-30. DECLARED, not observed, which makes it the sibling of samlSingleLogoutService rather than of wsfedReplyUrl: a cleanup is sent when a SESSION ends, and by then the request that would have carried a wreply is long over.  **A DECLARED ADDRESS OUTRANKS AN OBSERVED ONE** (#747). `cleanupTargetsFor()` pings every value here for a realm the session signed into, and the wreply the sign-in response went to, which `session.wsfedRealms` records, only where this is empty. From by hand. |
| `wsfedSpInitiatedSso` | one | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.704` | TRUE or FALSE: is this relying party's own wsignin1.0 answered, overriding wsfed.spInitiatedSso. A wsignin1.0 is an unsigned URL, so FALSE closes the door rather than proving who opened it. From the console, the management API, or by hand. |
| `wstrustAppliesTo` | several | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.705` | THE APPLIESTO ADDRESS from a RequestSecurityToken — the service the token is issued FOR, and WS-Trust's identifier attribute. Accumulates.  **IT IS READ**, which it was not before 2026-08-27, and it is `oauthAudience`'s exception arriving through a second protocol: an OnBehalfOf or ActAs asking for a token to reach `https://esb.example.com` is recorded on /admin/delegation against the APPLICATION that registered that address, so a chain of delegated hops draws as one picture rather than as boxes named after URLs that nothing else in it mentions. In development a LOOKUP and not a permission — an AppliesTo nobody registered is issued for and recorded verbatim; in product it is refused (#496). See forAppliesTo(), which asks this attribute first and `samlEntityId` behind it. From WS-Trust. |
| `wstrustJwtScope` | several | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.706` | Families: wstrust. THE OAUTH 2.0 SCOPES A WS-TRUST JWT FOR THIS APPLICATION CARRIES, one scope value each (#485). A JWT WS-Trust issues with this application as the AppliesTo (wst:TokenType urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:jwt) carries them in its `scope` claim, space-delimited (RFC 9068 section 2.2.3); with none set it carries no `scope`. A SAML token is unaffected.  **EACH IS JUDGED AS AN OAUTH ACCESS TOKEN'S IS**, with this application as the client: `oauthAllowedScope` declares what it may be issued (in product; this service's protected scopes in every mode), and the issuance policy's per-scope question decides. A value the policy drops is LEFT OFF the token and audited (STS-OAUTH-0579), never issued. A write naming an undeclared scope is accepted here, because the declaration may change and development grants undeclared scopes: declare it on oauthAllowedScope too. A value the policy will drop is WARNED about where it is set (#488): beside this field, in the Save reply, and as `warnings` on the /admin-api write replies and the application's view. From by hand. |

THE KEY TABLE: one JSON row per key this relationship decrypts with — its kid, its key type, `current` or `previous`, its certificate and chain under this realm's Intermediate, and the private key, SEALED under the key-encryption key wherever keys persist. A `previous` row is kept until its retiresAt and then removed by the scheduler job federation.encryption-key-retire. Written only by create, rotate and that job; WITHHELD from every LDAP search in product and from every page and /admin-api reply, which publish the public half. The key type is a column so a hybrid post-quantum key can be a row beside the classical one once one is registered. From this register. |
| `fedEncryptionKeyType` | one | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.101` | THE KIND OF KEY A PARTNER ENCRYPTS TO: rsa-3072 (the default for SAML 2.0 and WS-Federation) or ec-p256 (the default for OpenID Connect) — or, for OpenID Connect only, a post-quantum one (#82): x-wing (HPKE-10-KE, ML-KEM-768 + X25519) or ml-kem-768 (ML-KEM-768), an AKP key published in the relationship's JWKS with no certificate, from Internet-Drafts few partners implement yet. Changing it issues a new key of that kind at once and keeps the old one for federation.encryptionKeyGraceS, as a rotation does. From this register. |
| `fedEndSessionUrl` | one | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.102` | THE PARTNER'S OpenID Connect end_session_endpoint (RP-Initiated Logout 1.0), from its discovery document. When a person signs out HERE, the sign-out page offers to send them there with the partner's own ID Token as id_token_hint, this relationship's client_id, and this relationship's single logout endpoint as post_logout_redirect_uri — which the partner must have registered. The ID Token is kept on the session only while this is set. Empty: the partner is not told. From this register. |
| `fedFirstSeen` | one | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.103` | GeneralizedTime: when this relationship was first USED, which is not when it was created. From this register. |
| `fedHomeRealmDomain` | several | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.104` | HOME-REALM DISCOVERY (#148): an authorization request whose OpenID Connect Enterprise Extensions `domain_hint` is one of these goes straight to this partner's sign-in, unless the application names a partner of its own. Compared case-insensitively and exactly. A routing hint only — who is ADMITTED is fedSubjectDomain's. From this register. |
| `fedId` | one | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.105` | THE KEY: a short name an operator chose, unique across both roles. It is the RDN as well, unlike an application's, because this register is CONFIGURED rather than observed — nobody has to accept whatever a protocol presented, so the id can simply be required to be RDN-safe and short. From this register. |
| `fedIdTokenSignedResponseAlg` | one | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.106` | OPENID CONNECT ONLY. THE ONE ALGORITHM the partner signs this relationship's ID Tokens and Logout Tokens with — what was registered at the partner as id_token_signed_response_alg (OpenID Connect Core 1.0 section 3.1.3.7 step 7, Back-Channel Logout 1.0 section 2.6). A token signed with any other is refused, even one the partner's key verifies. Empty, the default: any algorithm of the verifying key's family that federation.jwtAlgorithms allows. Set it: an empty one accepts a token signed by another of the partner's keys under another algorithm. From this register. |
| `fedInitiateLogin` | one | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.107` | OPENID CONNECT ONLY. TRUE answers this relationship's login initiation endpoint, /federation/initiate-login/{id}, which the partner registers as initiate_login_uri (OpenID Connect Core 1.0 section 4): a sign-in the PARTNER starts, naming itself in iss, which must be fedPeer. A login_hint is passed on, and a target_link_uri is followed only to a path on this service. FALSE, the default, refuses it: a page anywhere could otherwise start a sign-in in a person's browser. From this register. |
| `fedJwks` | one | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.108` | The partner's public keys as a JWKS document, verbatim. Read BEFORE fedJwksUri and never refreshed, so a relationship carrying this makes no outbound request for keys at all. From this register. |
| `fedJwksUri` | one | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.109` | The partner's JWKS. FETCHED — which is the exact opposite of what oauthJwksUri on an application entry does, and the difference is the whole argument in federation_http.js: that one is a URL an unauthenticated caller REGISTERED, this one is a URL an administrator CONFIGURED. Leave it empty and paste the keys into fedJwks instead if this service is not to make the call. From this register. |
| `fedKeyId` | one | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.110` | APPLE ONLY: the id of the Sign in with Apple key, the kid of the client secret this service signs. From this register. |
| `fedKeyManagementAlgorithm` | one | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.111` | HOW THE PARTNER WRAPS OR AGREES THE CONTENT KEY, and the only one accepted. JOSE (an OpenID Connect ID Token): RSA-OAEP-256 or RSA-OAEP for an RSA key, ECDH-ES, ECDH-ES+A128KW or ECDH-ES+A256KW for an EC one. WARNING: RSA-OAEP is OAEP over SHA-1, offered for a partner that has nothing newer; RSA-OAEP-256 is the one to use. rsa-1_5 and RSA1_5 are refused in every mode (Bleichenbacher). Empty means the default for the key type. From this register. |

From this register. |
| `fedLastErrorAt` | one | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.113` | GeneralizedTime for the line above. Separate, so that an old error beside a recent success reads as history rather than as the current state. From this register. |
| `fedLastSeen` | one | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.114` | GeneralizedTime, the most recent use. From this register. |

Set it to the entityID the partner was configured with: it becomes the Issuer of the outbound AuthnRequest, the WS-Federation wtrealm, the SAML 1.1 providerId, this relationship's SP metadata entityID, and the audience an inbound assertion must name — which is a REFUSAL since 2026-09-12, so a partner that knows this service by another name needs this set. TRUE answers /federation/webfinger/{id}, where a PERSON types an identifier (acct:user@host or a URL) and this service asks that host who the person's OpenID Provider is (OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0 section 2, RFC 7033). A WARNING: the host dialled is one a caller chose — this service's one argued exception of that kind among the federation requests, under the outbound policy (no internal address in product mode, no redirect, the cap). The issuer found must begin with fedPeer, which bounds it to the partner an administrator configured; the person is shown the issuer and continues only by pressing a button. FALSE, the default, refuses. From this register. |

| `spiffeCredentialStatus` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.438` | WHETHER THIS IDENTITY MAY STILL BE ISSUED A CREDENTIAL HERE, and this is the one group in this list whose name could be read as a claim the service does not make. **SPIFFE HAS NO REVOCATION** — `GET /spiffe` says so, and the Workload API's `crl` field is empty because empty is the conforming value, not because it is unimplemented. `spiffeCredentialStatus` is NOT a certificate status and nothing verifying an SVID consults it: it records the three things in the registry that end an identity's ability to get a NEW one — its registration entry deleted, its agent banned, its agent deleted — and the certificates already in the world go on verifying until they expire, exactly as SPIFFE intends. The reason is a sentence rather than a code because it is the only thing that explains a status a reader did not expect. `spiffeRevokedAt` is never cleared, which is `mfaLastAuthTime`'s rule: it is the history the current-state flag beside it deliberately does not keep. |

| Class | Origin | OID | Kind | Superior | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `stsPasskeyPolicy` | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.2.14` | structural | top | This service's class for a passkey policy: how passkeys behave in this realm. The entry is named by the PROFILE (`cn=default`). |

| Attribute | Values | Origin | OID | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `description` | several | RFC | `2.5.4.13` | What the profile is for, for the next person. |
| `stsPasskeyAdminEnrolment` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.591` | `off` BY DEFAULT. `on` lets an administrator holding the Admin Write console role enrol a passkey for a person this profile applies to, from the person's page on the console or /admin-api: the registration ceremony runs in the administrator's own browser, against an authenticator they hold (a security key to be handed over, say), under the person's user handle, and is verified exactly as the person's own registration is — attestation, algorithms and this policy's registration rules. Nothing made elsewhere can be imported. The key records which administrator enrolled it and when, and the person is told. Left out of a save, the built-in default is kept. |
| `stsPasskeyAggregateDevices` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.592` | ON BY DEFAULT: one "Use passkey" step whose request lists every one of the person's passkeys, and the browser offers whichever is present. Off, a person with more than one is shown a choice per passkey, by its name, and the request names only that one. |
| `stsPasskeyAllowUsernameless` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.593` | ON BY DEFAULT. On, the sign-in screen offers *Sign in with a passkey* and the username field's autofill, which ask the browser for any discoverable credential of this realm (WebAuthn Level 3 section 5.4, `allowCredentials` empty) and sign in the account its user handle names, with user verification required and checked. Off, neither is offered and a sign-in always names the person first. Replaces the setting webauthn.usernameless. |
| `stsPasskeyAttestationAlgorithms` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.594` | `none` BY DEFAULT: an attestation is accepted whatever it is signed with. Otherwise a list from post-quantum, ml-dsa-44, ml-dsa-65, ml-dsa-87, slh-dsa and composite-ml-dsa: a passkey registers only with a TRUSTED attestation that carries a certificate, whose statement signature and the signature on every certificate of its chain, from the leaf to the trust anchor, are each one the list allows (`post-quantum` allows any ML-DSA, SLH-DSA or composite ML-DSA signature). Self and none attestation are refused, having no certificate. With enforceAttestationAtSignIn on, every sign-in holds the passkey to it by what its registration recorded, so a passkey registered before the rule stops working. This is the attestation's algorithm, not the passkey's own (postQuantumRequired). Left out of a save, the built-in default is kept. |
| `stsPasskeyBackupEligibility` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.595` | `allow` (the default) accepts any passkey. `disallow` accepts only DEVICE-BOUND ones: a passkey whose authenticator says it may be backed up or synced (the BE flag, WebAuthn Level 3 section 6.1) is refused when it is registered and when it signs somebody in, so a synced passkey enrolled before the realm said no stops working too. BE never changes for a credential. |
| `stsPasskeyClientRules` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.596` | EMPTY BY DEFAULT: every client is offered the list as it stands. Otherwise up to 20 rules separated by `;`, each `<browser> on <system>`, where either side is a family as the passkey ceremony rows name it (`Chrome`, `Firefox`, `macOS`, `Android`) or `*` for any, optionally followed by a major-version range (`141`, `130-140`, `130-`, `-140`): `Firefox 140- on Linux; * on Android 13`. A passkey registration from a matching client offers the list less ML-DSA (ES256 and RS256 where that leaves none). Not applied where a classical passkey is not allowed — registrationMode pq-only, webauthn.pqcOnly, postQuantumRequired registration-and-sign-in, or at the sign-in step under postQuantumRequired sign-in — nor to the post-quantum lane, and the ceremony row says it was not. Left out of a save, empty is kept. |
| `stsPasskeyCredentialLabel` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.597` | EMPTY BY DEFAULT: the provider's name, else "Passkey" or "Security key". Otherwise this text, with {provider} and {kind} filled in, at most 60 characters. The person may rename it afterwards, as always. |
| `stsPasskeyDeviceBoundRequired` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.598` | OFF BY DEFAULT. On, an issuance to an application this profile covers waits until the sign-on session is bound to the browser's key, and is refused when the browser skipped that registration or the wait elapsed without a binding. A session that was never offered registration is not refused by this row. Refused while authn.deviceBoundSessions is off. |
| `stsPasskeyEnforceAttestationAtSignIn` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.599` | OFF BY DEFAULT. The attestation rules (the webauthn.attestation* settings: the policy, the AAGUID list, the certification level and FIPS) are checked when a passkey is registered. On, they are checked again at every sign-in against what was recorded then and the FIDO Metadata Service as it is now, so a key registered before a rule was tightened, or whose model was since reported compromised, stops signing anybody in. A key with no trusted attestation fails every rule that demands one. |
| `stsPasskeyEnforcePinLength` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.600` | OFF BY DEFAULT. On, registration asks the authenticator for its minimum PIN length (CTAP 2.1 section 12.4, the minPinLength extension), records it on the key, and refuses a key whose minimum is below the next row, at registration and at every sign-in. A key answers only for relying parties it was configured to tell (CTAP 2.1 setMinPINLength with this RP ID); every other key, and every platform or synced passkey, does not report, and is refused unless the row after next is on. |
| `stsPasskeyEnterpriseSerialAttribute` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.601` | EMPTY BY DEFAULT: no serial is checked. Set to an attribute of a person's entry (for example `serialNumber`, which may hold several values), a security key registers only with a TRUSTED enterprise attestation whose certificate names a device serial that is one of that person's values. Needs webauthn.attestation set to enterprise, and the vendor or platform configured to release enterprise attestation to this RP ID; without that the browser sends ordinary attestation and every registration is refused. |
| `stsPasskeyHintsPasskey` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.602` | The WebAuthn hints (Level 3 section 5.4.8) the portal's *Create a passkey* sends, in order, from security-key, client-device and hybrid, or none. They tell the browser which way of making the passkey to lead with. A hint may not contradict webauthn.authenticatorAttachment: client-device implies platform, security-key and hybrid cross-platform. |
| `stsPasskeyHintsSecurityKey` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.603` | The hints *Use a security key* sends, in order, or none. The button asks for a cross-platform authenticator, so client-device contradicts it and is refused. |
| `stsPasskeyHintsSignIn` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.604` | The hints a sign-in ceremony sends — the passkey step, the sign-in with no username and its autofill — in order, or none (the default: the browser offers every way it knows). |
| `stsPasskeyLanes` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.605` | `realm` (the default) follows webauthn.pqcAlongsideClassical. `both` gives this profile's people a classical and a post-quantum passkey side by side, each under its own user handle, wherever the realm's setting is off; `one` gives them one lane wherever it is on. webauthn.pqcOnly still means one lane. Refused as `both` with registrationMode classical-only. Left out of a save, `realm` is kept. |
| `stsPasskeyMinPinLength` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.606` | The shortest PIN a security key may be set to accept, as the key itself reports it, while the row above is on. Between 4 (CTAP 2.1's own floor) and 63. |
| `stsPasskeyPinLengthOnlyIfSupported` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.607` | OFF BY DEFAULT, which is the strict reading: while the PIN length is enforced, a key that does not report it is refused. On, such a key is accepted and only a reported minimum is held to the rule — so the rule then binds only keys configured to report to this relying party. |
| `stsPasskeyPostQuantumAllowCredentials` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.609` | `realm` (the default) follows the realm's webauthn.postQuantumAllowCredentials. Read only while postQuantumRequired requires a post-quantum passkey at sign-in. `narrow` names only the person's post-quantum (ML-DSA) passkeys in the passkey step's request, so a classical one is never offered, and a person whose device holds only their classical one sees the platform's own "no passkey found" message. `list-and-refuse` names every passkey they hold and refuses a classical one after the ceremony, with a page saying that this application requires a post-quantum passkey and where to add one; the person may then pick a passkey that will be refused. A person holding no post-quantum passkey is told before any ceremony either way. Left out of a save, `realm` is kept. |
| `stsPasskeyPostQuantumRequired` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.610` | `off` (the default) accepts a passkey whatever its signature algorithm. `sign-in` accepts only a POST-QUANTUM passkey, one whose algorithm is ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65 or ML-DSA-87 (RFC 9964), when it signs somebody in, as the first credential or as the second factor; a classical one may still be registered. `registration-and-sign-in` refuses a classical one at registration too, and enrolment then offers only ML-DSA. The algorithm decides, not the lane a key was created in. Refused while the realm offers no ML-DSA (webauthn.algorithms names none, and neither webauthn.pqcOnly nor webauthn.pqcAlongsideClassical is on). |
| `stsPasskeyPrecedence` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.611` | Which named passkey policy wins where several match: the lowest, from 1 to 1000. |
| `stsPasskeyRecoveryAssurance` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.612` | `any` BY DEFAULT IN DEVELOPMENT, `not-weaker` IN PRODUCT. Whether a way back into the account that asks for no passkey — a password reset link, an activation link, a recovery code, an emailed code or link — restores access for a person who holds one. `any`: at once. `not-weaker`: the first sign-in after it that is not a passkey sign-in reaches no application; the person registers a passkey that satisfies this policy and signs in with it. `operator-only`: as not-weaker, and the self-service doors (the forgot-password form, a recovery code or an emailed code or link at sign-in) are refused; only an administrator's reset link, generated password or activation link remains. Left out of a save, the built-in default is kept. |
| `stsPasskeyRegistrationAlgorithms` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.613` | `realm` (the default) offers the realm's webauthn.algorithms. Otherwise the signature algorithms a passkey registration offers to this profile's people, in order of preference (an authenticator makes the first it supports), from the algorithms webauthn.algorithms may name. The next row may narrow or reorder it, and a passkey whose algorithm is not one this profile offers is refused when it is registered. Left out of a save, `realm` is kept. |
| `stsPasskeyRegistrationMode` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.614` | `realm` (the default) follows webauthn.pqcOnly and webauthn.pqcAlongsideClassical. `pq-only` offers only ML-DSA, and refuses a retry with the classical algorithms. `pq-first` offers ML-DSA first and the classical algorithms after it, even where the realm requests ML-DSA only. `classical-only` offers no ML-DSA and no post-quantum passkey beside a classical one, for people whose devices fail an ML-DSA registration. Refused with postQuantumRequired other than off or with attestationAlgorithms set (classical-only), and where the algorithms offered name no ML-DSA (pq-only, pq-first). Left out of a save, `realm` is kept. |
| `stsPasskeyRequireUsernameless` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.615` | OFF BY DEFAULT. It needs the row above. The realm's `default` profile does not apply it to the admin console, the debugger or the user portal; a named profile selecting that application does. |
| `stsPasskeyRpNameExtras` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.616` | `none` (the default) shows webauthn.rpName alone. `realm`, `organisation` or `realm-and-organisation` append the realm's name and/or saml.organizationName, so a person with accounts in several realms can tell the prompts apart. |
| `stsPasskeySecurityKeyResidentKey` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.617` | The `residentKey` an enrolment through *Use a security key* (or one that names no kind) sends WHILE usernameless sign-in is ON. While it is off the button always asks `required`, so it makes a discoverable credential as *Create a passkey* does (which asks `required` always). `discouraged` or `preferred` spare a security key's few resident slots, at the cost of a key that needs the username to sign in. Replaces the setting webauthn.residentKey. |
| `stsPasskeyUserDisplayName` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.618` | EMPTY BY DEFAULT: the name the sign-in knows, else the username. Otherwise up to six directory attributes in order, separated by commas; a group of attributes separated by spaces (givenName sn) joins their values. The first whose every attribute has a value becomes user.displayName (WebAuthn Level 3 section 5.4.3), with control and direction-changing characters removed and at most 64 characters. The username is always user.name. |

| `stsPasswordPolicy` | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.2.15` | structural | top | This service's own class, carrying the composition rules and the generated length the draft has no attribute for. The entry is named by the PROFILE: `cn=default`, or a named policy's name. |

| Attribute | Values | Origin | OID | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `description` | several | RFC | `2.5.4.13` | What the profile is for, for the next person. |

| `pwdInHistory` | one | other standard | `1.3.6.1.4.1.42.2.27.8.1.4` | How many of a person's PREVIOUS passwords are remembered and refused. The current password is always refused as well while this is above 0, so 5 means a new password may be none of the last six. 0 turns the rule off. The draft's attribute, with the draft's meaning. Each remembered password is kept as the hash it was already stored as (argon2id or scrypt), in pwdHistory on the person's own entry, and checking a new password costs one hash comparison per one remembered. |
| `pwdMinLength` | one | other standard | `1.3.6.1.4.1.42.2.27.8.1.6` | The shortest password this service will set, counted in characters (Unicode code points, so an emoji is one). The attribute is draft-behera-ldap-password-policy's. Twelve is the default; NIST SP 800-63B asks for at least 8, and 15 where a password is the only factor. |
| `stsPasswordPrecedence` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.620` | Which named password policy wins where several are named for one person: the lowest, from 1 to 1000. |
| `stsPwdArgon2Iterations` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.646` | How many passes argon2id makes over its memory (t). 2 is OWASP's minimum at 19 MiB; each pass adds the same time again. |
| `stsPwdArgon2Memory` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.647` | The memory one argon2id hash uses, in kibibytes (m). 19456 KiB (19 MiB) is OWASP's minimum and the least this service will write. Raising it makes a stolen store slower to attack, and every sign-in uses that much more memory. |
| `stsPwdArgon2Parallelism` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.648` | How many lanes argon2id divides its memory into (p). It is part of the hash, not a thread count: node computes a hash on one thread whatever this says. 1 is OWASP's figure. |
| `stsPwdGeneratedLength` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.649` | How long a password this service MAKES UP is — for a new user created from the console or /admin-api, an operator's Generate, and the product-mode bootstrap account. It must be at least the minimum length and at least twice the symbol count plus two. Twenty characters from a 90-character alphabet is about 130 bits. |
| `stsPwdHashAlgorithm` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.650` | The algorithm a newly stored password is hashed with: scrypt (RFC 7914), the default, or argon2id (RFC 9106, the OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet's first choice). A stored hash names its own algorithm and parameters and keeps verifying; one that is not in this algorithm with these parameters is hashed again at the person's next verified sign-in. Client secrets, activation tokens, recovery codes and app passwords are not passwords and stay scrypt. |
| `stsPwdMinSymbols` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.651` | Always 0. A policy that asks for symbols is refused: ASVS 5.0.0 6.2.5 requires that a password of any composition be accepted, so length is what this policy asks for. |
| `stsPwdRequireDigit` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.652` | Always off. A policy that requires a number is refused: ASVS 5.0.0 6.2.5 requires that a password of any composition be accepted. |
| `stsPwdRequireUppercase` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.653` | Always off. A policy that requires an uppercase letter is refused: ASVS 5.0.0 6.2.5 requires that a password of any composition be accepted. |
| `stsPwdScryptBlockSize` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.654` | scrypt's block size for a newly stored password while the algorithm is scrypt. Memory is about 128 × N × r bytes; 8 is the figure RFC 7914 and OWASP give. |
| `stsPwdScryptLogN` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.655` | scrypt's CPU and memory cost for a newly stored password while the algorithm is scrypt, as a power of two: 15 (the default) is N=32768. OWASP's table pairs it with the parallelism: 2^17 with p=1, 2^16 with p=2, 2^15 with p=3, 2^14 with p=5, or 2^13 with p=10. The default, 2^15 with p=1, is below it. |
| `stsPwdScryptParallelism` | not stated | this service | `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1.656` | scrypt's parallelism for a newly stored password while the algorithm is scrypt. Node computes it on one thread, so a higher value costs time rather than cores; the cost's description lists the pairs OWASP accepts. |
